title: date.today() and strftime() create dates and convert them to strings
body: date.today() uses the system's local date, and strftime formats a date as text. Fixed-width YYYYMMDD names sort well within one timezone, but servers in different timezones can produce different dates. Define the recording timezone first.
detail: date.today() uses the system's local date, and strftime formats a date as text. Fixed-width YYYYMMDD names sort well within one timezone, but servers in different timezones can produce different dates. Define the recording timezone first.

title: strptime() parses a date string into a date object
body: datetime.strptime() is a function that converts a date string, such as '2026-06-03', into an actual date and time object according to a specified format. To perform the calculation, the text must first be interpreted as a date.
detail: Even though a string representing a date may look like a date, it is simply text. To sort dates, calculate the difference between dates, or filter by date range, you must convert it to a `datetime` object using `strptime()`. If the string format and format code do not match, a ValueError may occur, so you should check both the input examples and the format.

title: `timedelta` represents a date difference, such as "a few days ago" or "a few days from now."
body: `timedelta(days=7)` represents a period of 7 days, and by adding or subtracting this value from a date, you can safely calculate dates a certain number of days before or after that date. It is also frequently used in filters for recent records.
detail: Use `timedelta` for tasks that require calculating date differences, such as organizing backup files, filtering data from the last 7 days, or calculating expiration dates. It’s safer to perform calculations using date objects rather than subtracting date strings directly. A good approach is to first convert the string to a date, and then create a `timedelta` object based on that date.

title: Distinguishing between UTC and KST helps reduce the problem of dates being off by a day.
body: Since the server time may be in UTC while users see KST, clearly distinguishing time zones can help minimize issues where dates are off by a day. Also, specify the recording standard, and distinguish between the storage standard and the display standard.
detail: For services or learning records based on Korean standards, the date in KST may be important. In Python, you can create a fixed KST offset using `timezone(timedelta(hours=9))`, and you must clearly specify the reference time when saving records. Distinguishing between storing data in UTC and displaying it in KST reduces confusion in production environments.
